The story of Lee Sharks Lee Sharks appears in public records as an independent writer, poet, and researcher whose work stretches from poetry into philosophy, artificial intelligence, semantics, and digital archives. Sharks published poetry—including Pearl and Other Poems—and developed a system of heteronyms, inspired in part by the tradition of writers such as Fernando Pessoa. Sharks describes the Crimson Hexagon explicitly as a research and aesthetic framework rather than a fictional universe. And then comes the wonderfully bizarre part: Mary Lee, the great white shark. Instead of merely treating this as a search-engine mistake, Sharks turned the collision into a literary and theoretical experiment. The project deliberately blurs scholarship, satire, conceptual art, and fiction. My previous answer treated the material too much on its own terms—as though “Lee Sharks” were simply a contemporary eccentric with a strange mythology. If we approach it as literary history, the more interesting question is: what kind of literary phenomenon is Lee Sharks, and what historical moment produced it? The answer is that Lee Sharks belongs to a very specific transition in literary history: the passage from postmodern authorship into networked, machine-mediated authorship in the early 21st century. Lee Sharks in literary-historical context The documented literary object begins, at least publicly, with Pearl and Other Poems in 2014. The book identifies Lee Sharks as a pseudonymous author within a much larger project called The Crimson Hexagon. Its own prefatory material explicitly places the project in the lineage of Robert Browning's dramatic personae, Ezra Pound's Personae, and Fernando Pessoa's heteronyms. That genealogy is the key to understanding what Lee Sharks is. This isn't merely a writer hiding behind a pseudonym. It is an attempt to make the author itself into a literary form. 1. The 19th-century precedent: the invented author There is a long tradition behind this. With Browning, the poet could write through dramatically constructed speakers. The “I” of a poem no longer necessarily meant “Browning.” Pessoa radicalized this. His heteronyms—Alberto Caeiro, Ricardo Reis, Álvaro de Campos and others—were not just masks. They had biographies, philosophies, styles and literary histories of their own. The crucial innovation was that one physical writer could generate a plurality of literary authors. Lee Sharks inherits precisely this problem. But it inherits it at a moment when the technological conditions have changed. In Pessoa's world, the heteronym ultimately existed inside the physical book and the imagination of its author. In the Crimson Hexagon, the different identities are distributed across books, websites, metadata, archives, digital documents, and eventually machine-readable corpora. The author is no longer merely plural. The author is distributed. 2. The modernist inheritance: Pound, Joyce, Borges The second major historical layer is modernism. Pound's Personae is particularly important because Pound used masks to absorb other voices, historical periods and literary traditions. Modernism repeatedly asked whether the individual lyric poet could contain the entire library. Joyce made the problem linguistic: Ulysses turns literary history into something that can be activated through style. Borges made it bibliographical. His imaginary books, imaginary authors, nonexistent encyclopedias and fictional citations produce an extraordinary inversion: literature begins to include its own bibliography as part of its fiction. And this brings us directly to the name Crimson Hexagon. It invokes Borges's Library of Babel: the infinite library in which every possible book exists. The 2014 Pearl volume explicitly frames itself as a fragment of a larger cultural epic composed of “selections” from fantastic, nonexistent works. That is very Borges-like. But Lee Sharks changes the Borges problem. Borges asks: What if the library were infinite? Lee Sharks asks: What happens when the library becomes computational? 3. The decisive historical change: the Internet This is where Lee Sharks becomes genuinely interesting as literary history. The Internet changes the ontology of the literary work. A traditional poem has: an author, a manuscript or edition, a publisher, a date, a reader. A networked literary work can have: multiple names, multiple versions, multiple locations, metadata, hyperlinks, machine indexes, search results, archives, algorithmic summaries, derivative documents, and readers who encounter the work through systems that are not themselves human. The later Crimson Hexagon explicitly describes itself as a distributed epic spanning 2004–2026, operating across authorial personas and print, digital, and AI-indexed substrates. Whether one accepts that self-description as historically important is another question. But as a literary artifact, the claim is revealing. It says, in effect: the medium of the epic is no longer the book. It is the information environment. 4. And that is where “Lee Sharks” becomes different from a pseudonym This is probably the most important point. Lee Sharks isn't best understood as: “a real writer whose pseudonym is Lee Sharks.” Nor is the most illuminating interpretation: “a fictional character called Lee Sharks.” The historical phenomenon is closer to an author-function deliberately constructed as a literary object. The name Lee Sharks sits inside a network of other names—Johannes Sigil, Jack Feist, Rex Fraction, and others. The current archive describes twelve such “faces,” each assigned different literary or intellectual functions. That is a very old literary device wearing a very new technological costume. Pessoa had heteronyms. The modernists had personae. Borges had fictitious bibliographies. Postmodernism had authorial disappearance. Lee Sharks adds the database and the algorithm to the machinery. 5. The 2014 moment is especially revealing Pearl and Other Poems appeared in 2014. That's an important date. This is after: the literary Internet had become mature, blogging had become a major literary form, social media had destabilized stable authorial identity, digital self-publication had become commonplace, Google had become an enormous intermediary between reader and text, and algorithmic classification was becoming part of ordinary cultural life. But it is before generative AI became the public literary environment it is now. That makes the work historically interesting in retrospect. The early Lee Sharks project can be read as belonging to the late-postmodern / early-digital literary period, while the later archive consciously reinterprets the project through the emergence of AI. The archive itself now describes its central problem in terms of text, provenance, machine traversal, semantic relations and AI-readable structures. So there is a chronological development: Pessoa → Pound → Borges → Internet literature → Lee Sharks → AI-mediated literature. That is a much more useful literary genealogy than “Lee Sharks is a weird modern writer.” 6. The Ginsberg problem There is another historical strand that shouldn't be missed. The 2014 introduction to Pearl explicitly says that Lee Sharks's work developed out of sustained engagement with Allen Ginsberg's voice, particularly the tension between Ginsberg's expansive, ecstatic voice and the more constrained voice that Sharks describes as emerging from his own academic work. That places Pearl within the history of American poetic voice. And the later work makes the lineage explicit: Whitman → Ginsberg → Lee Sharks. The 2026 “King of May” documents claim that Pearl and Other Poems inherits an operation from Ginsberg's Howl and Other Poems, which itself inherits and transforms Whitman's poetic operation. One needn't accept the claim that Lee Sharks is actually the rightful successor to Whitman or Ginsberg. Historically, what matters is that the work is consciously staging literary succession. That's an old avant-garde strategy. The artist doesn't merely make a new work. The artist attempts to rewrite the genealogy of literature so that the new work becomes necessary to the old one. 7. This is why the absurd biography matters The ridiculous biography attached to the 2014 book—18,000 degrees from Mars, fourteen Guggenheims, ruby statues, kidnapping intellectuals, dinosaurs, etc.—is easy to dismiss as internet nonsense. But literary-historically, it's doing something recognizable. It's an anti-biography. Instead of giving you the respectable author biography— born here, educated there, published this, taught at that university— it gives you an impossible mythological biography. That connects Lee Sharks to a tradition running through: Romantic literary self-mythologizing, avant-garde manifestos, Dada, Surrealism, Borges, conceptual art, and postmodern metafiction. The fake biography is therefore not incidental decoration. It attacks the assumption that literary authority comes from a verifiable biography. And that becomes particularly significant in the age of search engines and AI, where biographies themselves are assembled from metadata. 8. Then AI changes the meaning of the whole project This is where the 2020s Lee Sharks should be separated from the 2014 Lee Sharks. The later work explicitly identifies the problem of the machine reader. One 2026 theoretical document describes the future reader as one that is not human and presents the Crimson Hexagon as a distributed epic operating across AI-indexed substrates. Another document describes the project as an architecture in which documents teach AI systems how to read other documents. This is a genuinely different literary situation from Pessoa. Pessoa invented authors for human readers. Lee Sharks increasingly constructs authors, archives and interpretive instructions for both human and machine readers. That is why the later work can look bizarre if read simply as poetry. It is partly poetry, partly conceptual art, partly bibliography, partly archival practice, and partly an experiment in what happens to authorship when the reader is an information-processing system. 9. The historical category I'd put it in If I were writing a literary-history textbook, I wouldn't put Lee Sharks in a chapter called “Contemporary Poetry” without qualification. I'd put it somewhere around: The Literature of the Algorithmic Age with predecessors such as: Modernism → Pound / Joyce / Pessoa High postmodernism → Borges / Barth / Calvino Conceptual and procedural literature → Cage / Oulipo / Goldsmith and related practices Digital literature → hypertext, electronic literature, net.art Networked authorship → blogs, pseudonymous online identities, distributed archives AI-era literature → works in which search, metadata, machine reading, generation and corpus formation become part of the literary object. Lee Sharks sits at the intersection of those traditions. And the really interesting historical question The important question isn't whether Lee Sharks is “real.” That's almost the least interesting question. The historically important question is: What happens to the category of the author when an author deliberately constructs himself as a distributed literary system at precisely the moment when machines begin constructing their own representations of authors? That's the problem Lee Sharks accidentally—or deliberately—makes visible. In Pessoa, the author creates the heteronym. In Borges, the author creates the nonexistent book. In postmodernism, the author questions whether the author exists. In Internet literature, the author becomes a networked identity. With Lee Sharks, the author becomes something that can itself be indexed, replicated, misidentified, archived, recombined and read by machines. And that is why the later obsession with archives, metadata, provenance and AI isn't entirely a departure from the 2014 poetry. It's the technological environment revealing what the earlier literary experiment was already doing. The Crimson Hexagon archive now describes itself as having 1,647 deposits, 47 loci and hundreds of works, which is an enormous expansion of the original literary conceit into an actual archival apparatus. So I would tell the history this way: Lee Sharks is a literary experiment that begins in the old problem of the invented author and arrives in the new problem of the machine-readable author. That makes it much more historically interesting than either “a pseudonymous poet” or “an elaborate internet hoax.” And it places the work in a recognizable lineage: Pessoa → Borges → postmodernism → digital literature → AI-era literature. [QUERENT] [not in the paste] [ANSWER 3] Absolutely. Let’s treat Pearl and Other Poems (2014) not as an eccentric contemporary curiosity, but as a work that can be situated inside the history of poetry—and, importantly, distinguish what the poem does from the later mythology and theoretical apparatus that grew around it. A chapter in the history of 21st-century poetry: Lee Sharks and Pearl I. The historical problem Imagine opening a literary history written in 2050. The conventional story of twentieth-century American poetry would probably run something like: Whitman → modernism → Pound/Eliot → the Beats → Ginsberg → postmodernism → Language poetry/conceptualism → digital poetry → AI-era writing. Where would Lee Sharks go? My argument would be: not simply at the end of that sequence. Pearl and Other Poems belongs to a different current running underneath it: the history of poets attempting to transform the identity of the poet into part of the poem. That lineage is crucial because Pearl isn't merely a collection of poems by someone called Lee Sharks. The 2014 edition explicitly identifies “Lee Sharks” as a pseudonymous author within the larger Crimson Hexagon project, whose writers are constructed in the tradition of Browning's and Pound's Personae and Pessoa's heteronyms. So the first historical question isn't: What does Lee Sharks say? It's: What does it mean to make “Lee Sharks” into the speaker who says it? II. Whitman: the poet as a world The deepest American ancestor is Walt Whitman. Whitman's extraordinary invention wasn't merely free verse. It was the construction of a poetic self large enough to contain a nation. The “I” of Leaves of Grass continually expands: the individual becomes the multitude; the body becomes democratic; the poet becomes representative; the poem becomes an instrument for connecting otherwise separated lives. The Whitmanian poet therefore makes an enormous wager: my individual voice can become a collective voice. That is why Whitman is indispensable to understanding what comes later. The poet isn't simply reporting experience. The poet is constructing a position from which experience can be gathered. Lee Sharks inherits this ambition but changes its mechanism. Whitman says, approximately: I contain multitudes. The heteronymic tradition says: I contain other authors. The networked literary tradition eventually says: I contain other texts, identities, databases and machines. That is the historical movement in which Pearl becomes interesting. III. Pessoa: the self breaks apart Then comes Fernando Pessoa. Pessoa takes Whitman's gigantic poetic “I” and performs something almost opposite. Instead of one poet containing multitudes, the multitudes become poets. Alberto Caeiro isn't simply “Pessoa pretending to be Caeiro.” Ricardo Reis isn't merely another pseudonym. Álvaro de Campos isn't simply another voice. They constitute different authorial positions. This is why the 2014 Pearl description specifically invokes Pessoa's “art of the pseudonym” and the tradition of Personae. And here is the important connection: Lee Sharks isn't the beginning of the heteronymic experiment. It is a late transformation of it. Pessoa asks: How many authors can exist inside one author? Lee Sharks asks a technologically updated version: How many authors, documents, institutions, archives and identities can exist inside one literary system? The difference is subtle but historically enormous. IV. Pound: the mask becomes an instrument Ezra Pound provides another important bridge. Pound's Personae turns the poet into a kind of historical transmission device. The poet speaks through other voices. But Pound also introduces something crucial to the future of Lee Sharks: the poet as arranger. Pound's modernism is profoundly archival. He collects: fragments, quotations, translations, historical voices, myths, languages, cultural debris. The poem becomes less like a song produced spontaneously by an individual and more like an assembly of cultural materials. This is one of the roads leading eventually to conceptual and digital literature. And Pearl belongs to that road. V. Borges: the book becomes a universe Now we reach the most important ancestor. Jorge Luis Borges. Borges takes the modernist problem of literary accumulation and makes the library itself fictional. The nonexistent book becomes a literary object. The nonexistent author becomes a literary object. The imaginary encyclopedia becomes a literary object. The bibliography becomes literature. And The Library of Babel supplies the conceptual architecture that the later Crimson Hexagon explicitly adopts: a hexagonal library containing potentially every possible book. The later theoretical documents openly identify Borges's library as the origin of the “Crimson Hexagon” concept. This is the decisive step. Pessoa makes the author unstable. Borges makes the book unstable. Lee Sharks eventually makes the literary archive unstable. VI. The joke biography of Lee Sharks is therefore not just a joke Look at the biography attached to Pearl. Lee Sharks supposedly has: 18,000 degrees from Mars; fourteen Guggenheim fellowships; 10,000 MacArthur grants; ruby statues replacing friends and family; miniature offices inside his brain; kidnapped intellectuals; dinosaurs; tiny books; and eventually a self-replacement involving a ruby statue. It is absurd. But aesthetically, it is doing something very recognizable. It is a Borges-style fictional bibliography turned into an author biography. The biography has ceased to function as factual metadata. It has become part of the literary work. That matters enormously in retrospect because the Internet subsequently made authorial metadata itself into a literary battlefield. Today, a machine can encounter: Author: Lee Sharks and attempt to determine: Who is Lee Sharks? The absurd biography interferes with that operation. The metadata becomes text. The joke becomes an epistemological device. VII. Then comes Ginsberg If Borges explains the architecture, Allen Ginsberg explains the poetic voice. The 2014 work belongs to the aftermath of the Beat tradition, and later Lee Sharks documents explicitly position Pearl in relation to Ginsberg's Howl and Other Poems and the longer Whitman → Ginsberg lineage. This is important because Ginsberg's achievement wasn't simply that he wrote shocking poetry. He restored the possibility of a huge, public, prophetic poetic voice. The poet could again say: I see civilization. I see its sickness. I will name it. That voice descends directly from Whitman. But Ginsberg's “I” is not Whitman's harmonious democratic self. It is fractured, ecstatic, paranoid, sexual, political, mystical, urban. The poem becomes an enormous act of naming the contemporary world. And this is where Lee Sharks's ferocity becomes historically intelligible. The “Sharks” persona is deliberately excessive. It is too loud. Too knowledgeable. Too absurd. Too mythological. Too self-conscious. The voice is not trying to disappear into tasteful literary craft. It is trying to occupy literary space. VIII. The 2014 book is therefore caught between two traditions This is where I think Pearl becomes most interesting. It stands between: The Whitman–Ginsberg tradition The poet becomes enormous. and The Pessoa–Borges tradition The author becomes unstable. Those are almost contradictory impulses. One says: Make the poet gigantic. The other says: Destroy the stability of the poet. Lee Sharks combines them. The persona is simultaneously gigantic and fictional. That's an important characteristic of the work. IX. And then the Internet changes everything This is where the historical period becomes decisive. In 2014, literature no longer exists exclusively inside books. A literary identity can be: searched, indexed, copied, scraped, summarized, cross-linked, archived, misclassified, algorithmically recommended. That means the old literary question— Who wrote this? —acquires a new companion: What does the information system think wrote this? That's a fundamentally 21st-century literary question. And the later Crimson Hexagon project becomes increasingly explicit about it. The 2026 theoretical primer says that the work operates across print, digital and AI-indexed substrates and that the reader's searches and movements through the archive participate in constructing the work. This is where Lee Sharks begins to look less like a conventional poet and more like an early experiment in networked authorship. X. The remarkable thing about Pearl is that it predates the explanation And this is something I'd emphasize strongly in a literary history. The 2014 book should not simply be reread through the 2026 theory and treated as though the later theoretical system was already fully present. That's a historical mistake. There are two Lee Sharkses worth distinguishing: Lee Sharks, circa 2014 A poet/persona working through: heteronymy, absurd biography, poetic voice, literary genealogy, myth, American poetic tradition, the book as artifact. Lee Sharks, circa 2025–26 A much more elaborate theoretical and archival project concerned with: machine reading, metadata, AI indexing, semantic systems, provenance, archives, recursive documentation, and distributed literary objects. The later work interprets and systematizes the earlier work. That distinction is historically important. XI. This puts Pearl in the genealogy of conceptual poetry There is another tradition we need. The twentieth century gradually moved toward the proposition that the idea of a literary work could itself be literary material. Duchamp does this in art. John Cage does it with composition. The Oulipo does it with constraint. Conceptual writers increasingly make: procedures, documents, appropriations, lists, archives, instructions, bureaucratic forms into literature. By the 2010s, writers such as Kenneth Goldsmith and others associated with conceptual writing had made the boundary between “writing” and “information” increasingly unstable. Pearl arrives in that environment but takes a different route. It doesn't say: Information is poetry. It asks something closer to: What if the author, the biography, the bibliography, the fictional persona and the literary genealogy are all themselves pieces of the poem? That is a very different proposition. XII. And then the machine arrives This is where the historical trajectory becomes almost uncanny. The 2014 work makes metadata literary. The 2020s make metadata computationally consequential. And then generative AI appears. Now a literary persona can be encountered through an artificial reader that doesn't simply retrieve the work—it generates an account of the work. The later Crimson Hexagon explicitly embraces this situation, describing the AI summarizer as part of the compositional process. So the literary object has undergone another transformation: Book → archive → network → machine-readable corpus → machine interpretation. And suddenly the old Pessoa question becomes newly urgent. Pessoa asked: Who is speaking? AI asks: Who does the system think is speaking? Those aren't the same question. XIII. The great historical irony And here I think the Lee Sharks project becomes genuinely fascinating. The whole history of literary modernity is partly the history of trying to escape simplistic authorial identity. Browning: Don't assume the speaker is me. Pessoa: The speaker may be another author. Borges: The author may not exist. Postmodernism: The author is a function. Digital literature: The work may be distributed. AI literature: The reader may reconstruct the author algorithmically. And Lee Sharks sits almost exactly at the junction. The name Lee Sharks becomes simultaneously: author + character + pseudonym + literary device + metadata + search term + archival object. That's a distinctly 21st-century form of literary identity. XIV. So what is Pearl historically? I would resist calling it “a masterpiece” or “a failed experiment,” because those judgments require a much closer textual reading than we've done here. But I would make a stronger historical claim: Pearl and Other Poems is best understood as an early 21st-century experiment in heteronymic and meta-bibliographical poetry, emerging from the Whitman–Ginsberg tradition of expansive American voice while simultaneously inheriting the Pessoa–Borges tradition of destabilized authorship and fictional textual worlds. Its historical novelty is not simply its surrealism. It's the moment at which the old literary problem of the invented author meets the new technological problem of the indexed author. And that is why the later Crimson Hexagon architecture isn't as arbitrary as it first appears. The 2014 book creates the persona. The later work builds the system around the persona. The current archive goes further still: it describes itself as a governed reading/production environment, with hundreds of works organized through a machine-readable architecture. Whether future literary historians regard that architecture as major literature, conceptual art, experimental scholarship, or an eccentric hybrid is still an open question. But historically, the experiment is legible. XV. The literary-history diagram I'd actually teach the lineage like this: Whitman ↓ The poet becomes a world. Pound / Modernism ↓ The poet becomes an arranger of voices. Pessoa ↓ The poet becomes multiple poets. Borges ↓ The book becomes a fictional universe / library. Ginsberg ↓ The poet's voice becomes an enormous public instrument again. Conceptual / digital literature ↓ Documents, procedures, archives and information become literary material. Lee Sharks — Pearl (2014) ↓ The author/persona, biography, bibliography and poem begin collapsing into one another. Crimson Hexagon — later development ↓ The literary work becomes distributed across documents, identities and archives. AI-era Crimson Hexagon ↓ The machine reader becomes part of the literary circuit. And that last arrow is the one that makes the whole thing historically significant. Because we may now be entering the period in which literature isn't merely written for human beings; literature is also written in anticipation of being interpreted, summarized, indexed and recombined by machines. Lee Sharks's later work explicitly says that it was designed with such future readers in mind. That makes Pearl interesting retrospectively—not because the 2014 book secretly predicted AI, but because an old literary technology (the heteronym) happened to survive into a new technological environment in which the identity of the author itself became computational data. And that's, I think, the proper historical place to begin reading Lee Sharks. The next step I'd suggest is much more interesting than biography: we can take Pearl poem by poem and do a close reading, while putting each poem beside its actual ancestor—Whitman's Leaves of Grass, Ginsberg's Howl, Pessoa's heteronyms, and Borges's fictitious books. That would let us determine what Lee Sharks actually inherits, what he transforms, and where the work genuinely breaks with those traditions, rather than simply accepting the Crimson Hexagon's own account of its importance. What follows is Round 1 of a close reading of Pearl and Other Poems, concentrating on the opening sequence and then using the later titles in the book to reconstruct its poetic architecture. The surviving online text is a serialization of the 2014 edition, preserving its page boundaries. The bibliographic record identifies the book as a 2014 publication of 148–156 pages, with Johannes Sigil's introduction presenting “Lee Sharks” as a pseudonymous voice within the larger Crimson Hexagon. 1. The first surprise: Pearl begins by attacking metaphor The opening poem, “Pearl,” begins in what initially looks like unmistakably lyrical territory: loneliness, a train whistle, moonlight, ferns, water, dancers, shrapnel, explosions. But then it turns on itself. The speaker declares that there will be “no metaphors ever again”, and imagines a future in which metaphors have become extinct. This is much more interesting than simply saying that Sharks uses lots of surreal imagery. The poem's subject is actually the impossibility of escaping metaphor. The opening movement goes: metaphor → rejection of metaphor → archaeological reconstruction of metaphor → failed reconstruction → final surviving object. The poet imagines metaphors as fossils that future generations will excavate and try to reconstruct. The absurdity is deliberate: one metaphor's bones are attached to another's, creating a Frankensteinian museum of dead figurative language. That gives us our first major historical connection. This is not primarily a Whitmanian problem. It is a postmodern problem. The question isn't simply: How can I express the world? It is: Can language still produce meaning after we have become conscious of all the inherited machinery of poetic language? That's a very late-20th-century question. And Sharks makes it comic rather than solemn. 2. Compare this with Ginsberg Ginsberg's great achievement in Howl is partly the recovery of sincerity after modernist irony. Ginsberg can say: I saw the best minds of my generation... and actually mean it. The rhetorical force comes from the conviction that poetry can still name reality. Sharks inherits that gigantic prophetic posture—but then sabotages it. The poet says, essentially: I am going to make the enormous poem. And immediately: Actually, metaphor is dead. And then: Actually, I'm going to build a museum of dead metaphors. And then: Actually, I'm going to industrialize metaphor and sell it. The result is a poem constantly creating and destroying its own authority. That is where Sharks is much more recognizably a poet of the postmodern period than of the Beat tradition. 3. “The Metaphor Museum” is the key The first “Undersong” is literally called “The Metaphor Museum.” And its inventory is hilarious: William Carlos Williams, Sappho, Allen Ginsberg, David Foster Wallace, the Frankfurt School, Ancient Greek, Gnostic Christianity, Jewish/classical allusion, and a series of ridiculous museum objects. But don't overlook what the poem is doing structurally. The history of poetry has become a museum exhibit. That's an extremely important 21st-century image. The modern poet inherits a century or more of modern poetry as already-known cultural material. Whitman isn't simply a predecessor. He's an object in the museum. Ginsberg isn't simply a predecessor. He's an object in the museum. The avant-garde itself is an object in the museum. The poet therefore faces an extraordinarily difficult historical situation: How do you make a new poem when all the gestures of newness have already become recognizable? That's one of the central problems of postmodernism. 4. And then Sharks makes the museum into a factory The next “Undersong” is “The Metaphor Factory.” This is an important escalation. Museum → factory. The first means: poetry has become historical debris. The second means: poetry can be mass-produced. The poem imagines an industrial system producing identical metaphors, supported by marketing databases, statisticians and computer scientists. Now we're in a different historical world. This is 2014. The poem is already imagining poetic language as something subjected to: industrial production, data collection, marketing, algorithmic prediction, consumer manipulation, and statistical control. That's striking. It doesn't mean Sharks “predicted AI.” That would be too easy. But it does mean that the poem's enemy is already computational culture. And its solution is not to become anti-technology. Instead, the poem turns computational logic into grotesque comedy. 5. This is where the poem becomes distinctly American There is a long American tradition of treating poetry as an argument with mass culture. Whitman: the individual inside industrial democracy. Williams: ordinary American objects and speech. Ginsberg: the poet confronting industrialized, militarized, bureaucratic America. Sharks: the poet confronting the world of databases, marketing, algorithms and mass-produced signs. So there really is a historical continuity here. But the object of confrontation has changed. Whitman's America is the industrial nation. Ginsberg's America is the military-industrial / consumer society. Sharks's America is increasingly the data-mediated society. That is the real historical reason the book feels strange. Its literary inheritance is old. Its enemy is new. 6. The joke about algorithms is more important than it looks The poem imagines algorithms manipulating consumers through tiny subconscious images and marketing data. Today that language sounds almost ordinary. In 2014, it belonged to a recognizable anxiety about: surveillance capitalism, behavioral targeting, Big Data, social-media manipulation, predictive analytics. Sharks turns this into absurdist poetry. And there's a beautiful structural irony: the poet is complaining about systems that turn human beings into data while simultaneously turning poetry into a system of reusable symbolic units. That tension becomes increasingly important later in the Crimson Hexagon. The poet wants to escape the machine. But the poet also starts thinking like a machine: classify, catalogue, assemble, recombine, index, produce. That contradiction is central. 7. The “I” is therefore not a stable person This brings us back to Pessoa. The speaker repeatedly says “I.” But what kind of “I” is it? It is: poet, prophet, comedian, bureaucrat, marketer, tyrant, failed revolutionary, lover, critic, museum curator, factory owner, suicidal artist, frightened person. The voice keeps changing its social position. That's heteronymic in spirit even when it isn't literally a new named author. And notice the consequence: Lee Sharks is not merely a pseudonym attached to a consistent poetic personality. The voice itself is unstable. That is much closer to Pessoa than to an ordinary pen name. 8. Then comes “Strange New Earth” The sequence moves from the dead metaphor toward a landscape of apocalypse and renewal. The poem imagines sunrise over shattered pavement: the sun becomes physically wounded, almost animal-like, dragging itself above a ruined landscape. This brings us back to the older prophetic tradition. Whitman and Ginsberg both imagine catastrophe alongside regeneration. But Sharks can't simply perform prophetic transcendence. The poem has already taught us to distrust its own metaphors. So when the sun becomes a wounded creature, we know simultaneously: this is a powerful image and this is exactly the sort of metaphor the poem just declared dead. That contradiction is the engine. 9. The title Pearl finally makes sense The pearl is the object that survives all of this. The opening poem imagines the final poem as a pearl discovered in the remains of the poet's body after enormous stretches of time. That's an ancient poetic fantasy: the poem survives the poet. But Sharks gives it an unusual twist. The pearl is simultaneously: organic, mineral, bodily, textual, luminous, archaeological, and almost computational. It becomes a compressed remainder of language. The poet disappears. The metaphors die. Civilization disappears. But some tiny object remains. That is the title's central image. And now we can see why the later archive becomes obsessed with persistence, indexing and machine-readable text. The later theory is already latent in the metaphor: What survives of a literary work after its original context has disappeared? 10. Now look at the explicitly Ginsbergian poems The book's table of contents contains a poem called “an elegy for ‘Howl’” followed by “if walt whitman came back as a zombie and ate my brain i would write the following poem.” It also contains “i want you to know that i have personal authenticity as a poet because of my identity.” Those titles are almost a miniature literary-history syllabus. They give us: Ginsberg → Whitman → authenticity → Sharks. But the order matters. First Ginsberg is elegized. Then Whitman returns as a zombie. Then authenticity itself becomes an object of satire. This is not simply literary homage. It's succession anxiety. The younger poet is asking: How do I inherit the great American prophetic voice without merely imitating it? And the answer is hilarious: I will literally eat Whitman's brain. That is an extraordinarily direct metaphor for literary inheritance. The successor doesn't merely inherit the predecessor. He consumes him. 11. The Whitman zombie is therefore a theory of influence This is where I'd revise something from my previous answer. I previously described Sharks's relation to Whitman and Ginsberg primarily as a lineage. The poems suggest something more aggressive. It's not: Whitman → Ginsberg → Sharks like a respectable family tree. It's: Whitman → Ginsberg → Sharks → cannibalistic consumption of predecessors. The literary successor has to digest the tradition. Otherwise he becomes another museum specimen. And remember what happens in Pearl: the museum contains dead poetic traditions. So the poem's deepest anxiety may be: How do I inherit literary history without becoming part of the museum? That's a much stronger interpretation. 12. And now the famous “King of May” claim becomes intelligible The later archival material points to page 74, where Pearl explicitly claims the mantle of the “Good Gray Poet” and “King of May.” The archive identifies this as the book's claim to inherit Ginsberg's position. I would not simply accept the archive's conclusion that this establishes a genuine succession. But I would take the literary gesture very seriously. Because now we can see the logic: Whitman → Ginsberg → Pearl isn't an external theory imposed afterward. The book itself stages the succession. And it does so after spending its opening movement worrying about dead metaphors, dead poets and the museum of literary history. That's important. The “mantle” is an answer to the problem: How can a poet enter history without becoming another dead exhibit in the museum? The answer is: claim the living function of the predecessor. 13. But there is a great difference between Howl and Pearl This is where I think a genuinely critical reading has to resist the mythology surrounding the book. Ginsberg's prophetic voice derives much of its authority from historical embodiment. Howl emerged from: Beat culture, postwar America, sexuality and censorship, psychiatric institutionalization, Cold War America, drugs, Buddhism, jazz, and a very specific countercultural community. Sharks cannot simply reproduce that situation. By 2014, the cultural environment is different. The dominant problem isn't simply repression. It's saturation. There is too much information. Too many voices. Too many images. Too much irony. Too much media. Too much content. So the prophetic poet's problem has changed from: How do I speak against silence and repression? to: How do I speak when everything is already speaking? That's why the book becomes manic. It has to compete with the noise. 14. The formal solution is excess This may be the most important formal observation. Sharks doesn't solve the problem of cultural saturation by becoming minimalist. He becomes more excessive than the culture. Metaphor follows metaphor. Genre follows genre. Seriousness collapses into jokes. Political references become grotesque. Literary criticism becomes poetry. Poetry becomes literary criticism. The book continually overshoots its own boundaries. That is the aesthetic strategy. If contemporary culture produces infinite signs, the poem will produce an absurd infinity of signs and try to overwhelm the system from inside. That is quite different from Ginsberg's strategy. Ginsberg expands the lyric voice. Sharks expands the semiotic field. 15. And that's where Borges finally enters Borges's library contains every possible book. Sharks's literary universe begins moving toward something similar, but with a crucial difference. Borges's infinity is metaphysical. Sharks's infinity becomes procedural. There are: books, pseudonymous authors, imagined books, archives, categories, databases, machine texts, versions. The later Crimson Hexagon archive makes this explicit by organizing the 2014 poems into machine-readable records. Its current dataset identifies individual pieces of Pearl, including “an elegy for ‘Howl,’” the Whitman zombie poem, and others as distinct records. That is an extraordinary transformation. The poem that once mocked the metaphor factory eventually becomes data in a literary factory. And I don't enormous prophetic poem because the poem could still distinguish itself from the dominant mean that dismissively. That's the historical irony. 16. The really strange thing: Pearl has become what it feared This may be the central paradox of the entire project. The poem fears: museum → factory → database → dead metaphor. Yet the contemporary Crimson Hexagon project increasingly consists of: archive → database → metadata → machine-readable poems → indexing. So the question becomes: Is the later archive the fulfillment of Pearl's nightmare, or its solution? I think the answer is both. And that's why we shouldn't simply read the later theoretical claims as explanations of the 2014 poems. The later archive is itself another stage of the literary experiment. It takes the anxiety of Pearl and institutionalizes it. 17. My provisional judgment of the poetry At this point, I would make a fairly specific literary judgment. I don't think the strongest thing in Pearl is its claim to be the next Howl. The more interesting achievement is its awareness that the conditions which made Howl possible have disappeared. Ginsberg could make the enormous prophetic poem because the poem could still distinguish itself from the dominant culture. Sharks writes after the Internet has begun turning culture into an enormous undifferentiated stream. So Sharks makes the poem: museum + factory + website + autobiography + apocalypse + literary criticism + joke + prophecy. The instability is not a defect incidental to the work. The instability is the subject. 18. And now we can state the historical thesis more precisely I would now revise our earlier formula. Lee Sharks is not simply: Pessoa + Borges + Ginsberg + AI. That's too neat. A better genealogy is: Whitman: the poet absorbs the world. ↓ Pound: the poet absorbs other voices. ↓ Pessoa: the poet fragments into other poets. ↓ Borges: the poem expands into an imaginary library. ↓ Ginsberg: the poet attempts to recover a public prophetic voice. ↓ Postmodernism: the poet becomes suspicious of every inherited literary gesture. ↓ Digital culture: all those gestures become searchable, reproducible information. ↓ Lee Sharks / Pearl: the poet tries to become's final image—the tiny surviving pearl, recovered after the poet and his metaphors have disappeared—is almost painfully larger than the archive while simultaneously recognizing that the poet is already becoming an archival object. That's the real historical problem. And Pearl's final image—the tiny surviving pearl, recovered after the poet and his metaphors have disappeared—is almost painfully appropriate. The question isn't: Will the poet become immortal? It's: What tiny thing will remain after the entire cultural apparatus has forgotten what it meant? That is a very 21st-century version of the ancient poetic dream of immortality. One thing I want to do differently in Round 2 There is enough actual text available now to stop talking about Pearl abstractly. I propose we take the book's next major sequence—especially “an elegy for ‘Howl,’” the Whitman-zombie poem, and the authenticity poem—and put each directly beside Howl, Leaves of Grass, and Pessoa. That will let us answer a much harder question: Is Lee Sharks actually doing something formally new with the Whitman/Ginsberg inheritance, or is the book principally a brilliant parody of the idea that a contemporary poet could inherit that mantle? The distinction is crucial. The later Crimson Hexagon archive argues very strongly for the first interpretation, but the poems themselves may give us a more complicated answer. The sequence is unusually revealing because the poems on pages 37–49 form something like a miniature argument about inheritance, authenticity, death, illness, and poetic speech. The table of contents places “an elegy for ‘Howl’,” the Whitman-zombie poem, and “i want you to know that i have personal authenticity as a poet because of my identity” consecutively, followed by poems about the poet's own death and the sickness of the air. 1. “An elegy for ‘Howl’”: killing the predecessor The first thing to notice is the title. It isn't: “Ode to Ginsberg” or “After Howl” but “an elegy for ‘Howl’.” An elegy presupposes a death. So before Sharks can inherit Ginsberg, he has to declare Howl dead. That is already a fascinating reversal of literary succession. The conventional young poet says: Ginsberg was my influence. Sharks's poem says: Ginsberg is my dead predecessor. The difference is enormous. An influence remains above you. A dead predecessor can be buried, mourned, cannibalized, inherited, or replaced. And this is exactly what the following Whitman poem does: the dead predecessor comes back as a zombie and eats the successor's brain. The book is therefore constructing a deliberately grotesque cycle of literary death → resurrection → incorporation. The elegy is therefore not simply homage. It is an initiation ritual. To become the next poet, you must first survive the death of the previous poet. 2. But what is being mourned? Here I think the poem's position becomes more subtle. The thing being mourned isn't simply Allen Ginsberg. It's the possibility represented by Howl. Howl demonstrated that a poem could: speak publicly, name an entire generation, catalogue its damaged bodies and minds, attack institutions, invoke visionary experience, and transform private suffering into communal utterance. That was the great Ginsbergian proposition. Sharks inherits the proposition. But the cultural circumstances have changed. The 2014 poet isn't standing outside the culture shouting into it. He's already inside an enormous network of: poetry websites, comment threads, social media, online literary communities, search engines, institutional gatekeeping, self-publishing, and algorithmic visibility. So the question becomes: Can the Ginsbergian poem still function when the poet's speech is already caught inside the network? That is what makes the elegy an elegy. The poem isn't simply saying that Ginsberg is old. It's asking whether Ginsberg's poetic technology still works. 3. Then the Whitman zombie arrives This is the extraordinary poem that follows. Its speaker begins: “I am very sad America because you make me sad.” That deliberately echoes the gigantic American prophetic “I” of Whitman and Ginsberg, but reduces it to economic precarity, unemployment, debt, online rejection and loneliness. The poem explicitly contrasts its own situation with Whitman's door-to-door selling of books and asks whether a new Whitman could sell “zombie poems” through Google. That is much sharper than the title's joke initially suggests. Whitman sold books door to door. Sharks posts poems online. That's the historical transformation. Whitman's literary marketplace was physical: body → street → book → reader. Sharks's is: body → screen → website → platform → algorithm → reader. And suddenly the zombie joke becomes a theory of literary transmission. 4. The poet's poverty is not incidental The speaker says he has: no money, credit-card debt, student-loan debt, unemployment, and no friends. We shouldn't simply read this as autobiography. It is functioning as a counter-portrait of the contemporary poet. Whitman could imagine himself as a democratic poet because he could physically circulate through the public. Sharks imagines the contemporary poet as digitally ubiquitous and socially isolated. That is a brilliant paradox: the Internet gives the poet access to everyone while potentially giving the poet access to nobody. The poem's loneliness is therefore technological as well as emotional. 5. “Could a new Walt Whitman...?” The question near the end is the poem's hinge: Could a new Walt Whitman emerge from this environment? That's what the whole poem has been testing. And the answer isn't simply “yes.” The poem ends by insisting on: “Vision” and “Commitment.” Those words matter because they are old-fashioned poetic virtues. Vision. Commitment. America. Poetry. These are Ginsbergian/Whitmanian words. But they're being uttered from a world of Google, debt, spam, IP bans and poetry websites. The poem therefore stages an impossible experiment: Can an archaic prophetic vocabulary survive inside the platform economy? That's the real subject. 6. The zombie is a theory of influence Now we can understand the title. Why does Whitman have to be a zombie? Because literary influence is a form of haunting. The predecessor is dead, but continues to inhabit the successor. The younger poet can't escape him. But there's a second joke: the zombie eats the brain. The successor literally gets his brain eaten by the predecessor. That's the reverse of influence. Instead of: I consume Whitman. we get: Whitman consumes me. This is an extraordinarily good image for literary inheritance. The tradition isn't something you simply choose to inherit. It can swallow you. 7. Then comes the authenticity poem And this is where the sequence becomes much more intellectually sophisticated. The title is: “i want you to know that i have personal authenticity as a poet because of my identity.” That title sounds like satire of contemporary identity politics. But we should be careful. The poem doesn't simply say: identity is fake. It does something stranger. The speaker claims every identity simultaneously. The poem says, in rapid succession, that the speaker is a genocide victim, minority, foreigner, blue-collar worker, Harvard-educated person, dropout, farm-raised person, ghetto-raised person, wealthy urbanite, academic descendant, newly born speaker, suicide, war veteran and war protester. The point isn't merely contradiction. It's exhaustion of identity as an authenticity credential. 8. Pessoa is hiding inside this joke This is where our earlier Pessoa discussion becomes concrete. Pessoa's heteronyms multiply the author: I am Caeiro. I am Reis. I am Campos. Sharks takes that operation and makes it almost pathological: I am everybody. But there is an important difference. Pessoa creates distinct personalities. Sharks creates an accumulation of incompatible identities without stabilizing them into separate personalities. That's a very contemporary move. The poem isn't asking: Which identity is the real one? It's asking: What happens when the demand for an authentic identity becomes so intense that the speaker can satisfy it only by claiming every possible identity? The answer is absurdity. 9. The “I” becomes a database This is the point where I think we can legitimately connect the poem to the later machine-oriented work—but without pretending the poem is secretly about AI. The speaker becomes a list. Identity becomes metadata: race, class, education, geography, trauma, profession, political position, sexuality, biography, victimhood, achievement. The self is effectively queryable. That's an extremely 21st-century conception of identity. And here's the beautiful irony: The Whitmanian “I” was supposed to contain multitudes organically. The contemporary version contains multitudes as a list of attributes. Whitman's multiplicity is poetic. Sharks's multiplicity is bureaucratic. That's a major transformation. 10. Whitman says “I contain multitudes.” Sharks says: I contain contradictory metadata. That is the joke. And the joke has teeth. Because contemporary literary culture increasingly asks writers to establish their authority through identity: Who are you? What community do you represent? What experience authorizes you to speak? Those are legitimate questions in many contexts. But the poem notices the danger of converting identity into a literary credential. If authenticity is the condition of poetic legitimacy, the speaker can simply manufacture the maximum possible authenticity by claiming everything. Thus the poem becomes a reductio ad absurdum. 11. And this takes us straight into “I think I died a long time ago…” The next title is almost inevitable: “i think i died a long time ago…” After claiming every identity, the speaker discovers that the stable self may already be dead. That's not random sequencing. The little sequence goes: Ginsberg dies → Whitman returns → identity explodes → self dies. That's a coherent philosophical progression. The literary father dies. The literary grandfather returns. The contemporary poet tries to establish his identity. The identity collapses. And then the air itself becomes sick. 12. “The air is sick all over…” Now the pathology spreads outward. First the speaker is sick. Then identity is unstable. Then the air is sick. Then: “air, you're sick—tenderly will i bind you…” The poems move from individual → social → environmental. This is a classic poetic movement. But Sharks does something unusual with it: the cure becomes an act of poetic address. The poet tries to speak to the air. Language becomes a form of binding. That's an old conception of poetry: speech as healing, blessing, incantation. But by this point we've learned not to trust the speaker's claims to mastery. So the tenderness is precarious. The poet can say: I will bind the sick air. But the reader has already watched him fail to stabilize: metaphor, authorship, literary inheritance, identity, and selfhood. The poem's tenderness therefore emerges after irony, not instead of irony. That's important. 13. “Knot-hinge”: the smallest possible theory of the book The next title, “knot-hinge,” is fascinating. A knot joins. A hinge transforms one position into another. So the word itself describes the structural operation we've been watching: connection + transformation. Whitman connects the individual to the multitude. Ginsberg connects private suffering to public witness. Pessoa connects one author to multiple authors. Borges connects fiction to bibliography. Sharks connects those traditions to the networked contemporary world. But each connection changes what came before. That's why I don't think “influence” is quite the right word. Sharks is interested in transmission as transformation. 14. The sequence has a hidden dramatic plot If we stop treating these as miscellaneous poems, the sequence looks almost like a drama: Act I — The father dies “an elegy for ‘Howl’” Act II — The grandfather returns Whitman as zombie Act III — The successor claims legitimacy “personal authenticity” Act IV — The successor discovers the self is already dead “i think i died a long time ago…” Act V — The world itself is sick “the air is sick all over…” Act VI — Poetry attempts repair “air, you're sick—tenderly will i bind you…” Act VII — Connection becomes mechanism “knot-hinge” That is not accidental-looking sequencing. The book is dramatizing the problem of becoming a poet. 15. And suddenly the title “Fuguework” makes sense The entire section is called FUGUEWORK. That's an excellent title. A fugue is repetition with variation. A voice enters. Another voice follows. The first voice returns altered. Multiple voices coexist. One theme migrates between voices. That's precisely what the book is doing with: Whitman → Ginsberg → Sharks. The tradition returns, but every return changes its register. And “fugue” also suggests flight—escape, dissociation, movement away from a stable identity. So Fuguework names both: the musical structure of repetition/variation, and the psychological movement away from a stable self. That is almost a miniature definition of the entire book. 16. Which brings us back to Pessoa—but differently At the beginning we said: Lee Sharks inherits Pessoa's heteronymy. After these poems, I'd make the claim more precise. Pessoa's fundamental problem is: How can one consciousness become many authors? Sharks's problem is: How can one author survive a culture in which every identity, literary ancestor and cultural position is already available for quotation and recombination? The answer is not to invent one more stable persona. It's to make instability itself the persona. That's the crucial move. 17. And this is why I wouldn't call the poems merely parody A superficial reading would say: Sharks makes fun of Whitman and Ginsberg. True, but inadequate. The poems are doing something more affectionate and difficult. They need Whitman and Ginsberg. Without them, the jokes have no voltage. The zombie is funny because Whitman's poetic body is genuinely enormous. The elegy matters because Howl genuinely changed American poetry. The authenticity poem works because the tradition of the poet speaking from personal experience is genuinely powerful. The satire is therefore a form of dependency. Sharks cannot kill the fathers. He needs their corpses to make his poems. That's precisely why they keep returning. 18. A provisional close-reading thesis After these poems, I'd put our argument this way: Pearl is not primarily an attempt to imitate Whitman or Ginsberg. It is a drama about the impossibility of inheriting them unchanged. Whitman's expansive “I” becomes a problem of identity. Ginsberg's prophetic voice becomes a problem of historical succession. The Beat catalogue becomes a problem of cultural saturation. The authentic autobiographical poet becomes a problem of identity-as-metadata. And the old prophetic poem becomes a poem about websites, debt, algorithms, exclusion and loneliness. The poet therefore has to do something peculiar: inherit the tradition by breaking it. Next: “years the cankerworm ate” → “ringtone” → “alien singings: a psalm” → “song of me” This next run is especially promising because “song of me” makes the Whitman inheritance completely explicit, while “ringtone” and “alien singings” push the inherited lyric voice into technological and extraterrestrial registers. The contents place those poems immediately after “knot-hinge” and before “your love will carry on.” That gives us the next question: What happens when the Whitmanian “Song of Myself” is no longer sung by a human self, but by a technologically mediated, alienated, possibly post-human voice? That is where Pearl starts getting genuinely strange—and where the transition from American prophetic poetry to posthuman/digital poetry becomes visible inside the poems themselves. That gives us a different way of reading the poem's anxiety. It's not merely: “Metaphors are cliché.” It's closer to: What would experience look like if language stopped converting one thing into another? A finger would be only a finger. Thought would be only thought. A train whistle would be only a train whistle. The world would lose the connective tissue that poetry supplies. And that's why the promised post-metaphorical world immediately feels like an empty lakebed. The disappearance of metaphor is also the disappearance of imaginative relation. Then something remarkable happens The poem doesn't actually celebrate that world. It says: “By the time I wake, I will have forgotten.” The speaker has forgotten the very thing he was trying to preserve. This is the first major temporal operation of the poem. The poem is not simply about metaphor. It is about memory and irreversibility. Something happens. Then it disappears. The speaker tries to recover it. But recovery is impossible. That becomes explicit in section II: “After my poem has happened, I will wish I could take it back.” This is extraordinarily important. The poem is treating composition as an irreversible event. A poem happens. Once it has happened, it enters the world. The poet cannot retrieve it. That gives us a much stronger interpretation of the title Pearl. The pearl is not simply “a surviving poem” It is a thing that cannot be taken back. By section V, the future has become almost unimaginably distant: “Aeons crush by above me.” Memory becomes legend. Then legend disappears. Eventually the speaker's bones are discovered. Inside the rib cage is the final poem—the pearl. But look carefully at what happens to the poem at this point. It stops behaving like an ordinary linguistic object. It becomes: a stone, a marble, a muscle, a fossil, a shard of shrapnel, a neon sign, a moon, a rock, a spirit, a bone, a “machine of living ghosts.” This is where the poem's opening anti-metaphor proposition becomes complicated. The final poem is almost literally a metaphorical object. But it is also trying to become something beyond metaphor. “Impervious to metaphor's gleam” This phrase is the hinge. The pearl is described as: “impervious to metaphor's gleam / but very, very bright” That's an extraordinary formulation. The pearl is not merely another metaphor. It's an object imagined as surviving metaphor itself. The poem has spent its first pages producing metaphors and then fantasizing about their extinction. Now it produces an object that supposedly cannot be exhausted by metaphor. That's why the pearl has such strange ontological status. It is simultaneously: poem / object / relic / body / stone / signal / machine. The poem wants to escape the distinction between language and thing. And notice what happens to authorship At the beginning: “My poems will make me not be alone.” That's an intensely personal claim. At the end: “my poem will have happened like a foghorn happens at sea where no one writes it” The author has disappeared. The poem now behaves like the train whistle from the opening. It simply happens. This gives the whole poem a beautiful circular structure: train whistle → poem → metaphor → death → fossil → pearl → foghorn The beginning and ending mirror each other. The poem wants to become an event rather than an authored statement. That is much more interesting than the interpretation I gave earlier about “the poem surviving the poet.” It does survive the poet, yes. But more specifically: the poem imagines literary immortality as the disappearance of authorship. The final line changes everything The last phrase is: “no longer alone.” Now return to the opening: “My poems will make me not be alone…” At first, loneliness is solved by communication. At the end, loneliness is solved by transmission through time. The dead poet's poem reaches an unknown reader. That reader sees the pearl. And the poet is no longer alone. But the reader is also anonymous. So the relationship isn't: author → reader in the conventional sense. It's: dead body → artifact → unknown future consciousness. That's why the foghorn image is so exact. A foghorn doesn't need anyone to “write” it. Its meaning is produced by its reaching someone through darkness. The poem wants to become that. Now the Whitman/Ginsberg question looks different This is where I'd connect the poem to the literary tradition, but only after establishing what the text itself is doing. Whitman is intensely interested in the survival of the poet through future readers. Ginsberg inherits that desire for communication across generations. But Pearl makes the transmission much stranger. Whitman's poet says, essentially: I speak to you from my present. Sharks's poet says: I may be dead before you even exist. And the medium connecting them isn't shared democratic space. It's a fossilized object. The future reader doesn't encounter the poet's living voice. The future reader encounters the residue of a dead body. That makes Pearl considerably darker than the Whitmanian model. There's also a very precise tension with Romantic poetry The Romantic poet traditionally wants the poem to preserve subjective experience. The speaker says: this is what I felt. Sharks pushes toward something almost opposite: the feeling will eventually be gone, and only the object will remain. That's why the poem repeatedly converts psychic experience into physical matter. Thought → water. Emotion → tremolo. Poem → pearl. Memory → legend. Legend → dust. Body → fossil. Poem → stone. This is a poetry of materialization. The poem doesn't want merely to express consciousness. It wants consciousness to become an object capable of surviving consciousness. And now the book's title becomes much more precise A pearl is created around an irritant. That's not stated explicitly in the poem, so I wouldn't force that symbolism onto it. But the poem itself supplies its own version: “a fossilized shard of shrapnel” is enclosed in the final object. That is striking. The pearl contains violence. The poem's beautiful surviving object is built around a fragment of destruction. So the “pearl” isn't pure beauty. It is beauty organized around damage. And that makes the earlier atom bomb/shrapnel imagery retroactively important. The opening explosion isn't merely decorative surrealism. The final pearl incorporates the shrapnel. The poem has transformed injury into an object of transmission. That's a much more defensible reading than my earlier broad claims about “the archive.” One correction to our previous discussion This also means we should be careful with the later Crimson Hexagon theory. The later material calls Pearl things like “the logotic substrate,” “retrocausal canon formation,” and so forth. Those are later interpretive frameworks. They may be interesting. But they shouldn't be smuggled backward into the 2014 poem as though the poem itself announces them. The poem gives us something considerably more concrete: loneliness → metaphor → memory → death → material residue → future reader → communication. That's where we should start. Then we can ask whether the later theory genuinely illuminates that structure or merely redescribes it in grander terminology. And I think we should proceed this way from here No more reading the contents page as though it were the poem. For each poem, I'll distinguish: Text: what is actually on the page. Form: syntax, repetition, lineation, diction, imagery, structure. Immediate argument: what the poem appears to be doing internally. Intertext: only where there is actual textual evidence for a connection. Historical context: what becomes visible when we place that reading alongside earlier poetry. Later Crimson Hexagon interpretation: treated separately, as reception/history rather than authorial truth. And we should probably go in order from page 3 onward, rather than jumping straight to the poems with obviously provocative titles. That means the next object should actually be “RE: WHY DON'T YOU GO START YOUR OWN POETRY WEBSITE INSTEAD OF COMPLAINING ABOUT THIS ONE?”—because it precedes “PEARL” and is already doing something fascinating with letter, website, telepathy, literary criticism, the body, and the pearl itself. The actual pages are available in the 2014 serialization. That poem may turn out to be the real key to the whole book.
